objectives: Name the four lung volumes and four capacities, and explain why spirometry cannot measure residual air.
Read the air exhaled early and the total forced breath from two linked curves.
Explain how resistance and lung stretch affect illustrative curves, and why a fraction alone cannot establish lung size.
Check effort and test quality before interpreting a forced breath.

quiz.stem: Which air remains in the lungs after the strongest possible exhalation?
choices: Residual volume
Tidal volume
Inspiratory reserve volume
Expiratory reserve volume
quiz.why: Residual volume stays inside even after a maximal breath out. Expiratory reserve is the extra air that can be pushed out after a quiet breath out, so it does leave.

quiz.stem: Which combination of volumes makes vital capacity?
choices: Inspiratory reserve, tidal and expiratory reserve volumes
Tidal, expiratory reserve and residual volumes
Inspiratory reserve and residual volumes only
All four volumes, including residual
quiz.why: Vital capacity is all the movable air: both reserves plus tidal air. Adding residual air as well gives total lung capacity, the tempting wrong answer.

quiz.stem: Why can spirometry alone not measure total lung capacity or functional residual capacity?
choices: Both include residual air, which never passes through the mouthpiece
Both need a stronger breath than most people can give
Both depend on the speed of emptying, which spirometry cannot time
Both are defined by the first second of a forced breath
quiz.why: A spirometer sees only air that moves through it. Residual air stays inside, so another method, such as body plethysmography or gas dilution, is needed. Blowing harder does not release it.

quiz.stem: On a forced breath, what does the early exhaled volume (FEV1) measure?
choices: The air blown out in the first second
The air left inside after the breath
All the air in the lung
The air moved in a quiet breath
quiz.why: FEV1 is the early part of the total forced breath. The total forced breath is FVC; the ratio of the two is the fraction that leaves early.

quiz.stem: What is on the horizontal axis of a flow-volume loop, and which limb shows breathing out?
choices: Volume exhaled; the upper limb shows breathing out
Time; the upper limb shows breathing out
Volume exhaled; the lower limb shows breathing out
Pressure; the lower limb shows breathing out
quiz.why: The loop trades the time axis for exhaled volume, and outward flow draws the upper limb while the volume-time curve rises. The lower limb is breathing in.

quiz.stem: A forced breath shows slow early emptying and a low early fraction. Which pattern does this suggest, and what would confirm a restrictive pattern instead?
choices: Obstructive; a measured low total lung capacity defines restrictive
Restrictive; a low early fraction defines restrictive
Obstructive; a response to airway opening defines restrictive
Restrictive; a high early fraction alone defines restrictive
quiz.why: A low fraction suggests air has difficulty getting out, an obstructive pattern. A reduced measured total capacity is what defines a restrictive pattern, so the fraction alone cannot settle it.

quiz.stem: A person's early exhaled volume and total forced breath are both smaller than predicted, but their fraction looks preserved. What can be said?
choices: The fraction describes speed of emptying, so it cannot show that lung size is normal
The preserved fraction proves total lung capacity is normal
The preserved fraction proves the airways are blocked
The smaller volumes prove residual air is missing
quiz.why: Both volumes can fall while their ratio stays similar. A fraction describes how fast air leaves, not how large the lung is, so size must be read alongside it.

quiz.stem: A forced breath gives unusually low volumes and flows. What should come before naming a pattern?
choices: Check the quality of the effort and compare repeated acceptable breaths
Name the most likely disease straight away
Treat the lowest value as the true one
Ignore the curve and rely on the fraction
quiz.why: A forced test needs a deep breath in, a strong start and continued exhalation. Low effort can mimic an abnormal pattern, so quality comes first.

takeaways: A spirometer sees only moving air. Residual air stays inside, so residual volume and the capacities that contain it (functional residual capacity and total lung capacity) need another method.
Vital capacity is all the movable air: tidal volume plus both reserve volumes. Total lung capacity adds residual volume.
Read the total forced breath and the part exhaled early together. Their ratio is the fraction of the breath that leaves early.
The early fraction describes speed of emptying, not lung size. Obstruction slows emptying, while restriction is defined by a reduced measured total lung capacity.
More compliance means easier stretch, not necessarily better emptying. Resistance slows emptying, and the lesson's model curves are illustrative, not patient values.
Check effort and test quality before interpreting any forced breath: low effort can imitate disease.
A bronchodilator response measures a change. It is not a stand-alone diagnosis.
